items.title: Ed Shaughnessy Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 1, 1995 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Because we were good friends you know.

ctx.x: It would include the 60’s. I think I recorded with him over a period of about four years in the 60’s, and most of the time, this is going to sound very strange, but thank God for Sonny Payne’s marital problems, because when Sonny Payne his regular drummer couldn’t come into New York because his wife would throw him in jail, Basie would call me up. And I used to say to Sonny, “geez, Sonny, you’re my man but you know these marital problems are really groovin’ me.” And he would say some proper epithet, you know,…
I love it. We’ve got one over there for you to sign as a matter of fact.

items.title: Ed Shaughnessy Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 25, 1998 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: He said “I thought it was Sonny Payne.”

ctx.x: Oh yes. If I might interject it’s annoyed me that the two best albums I made with Basie were called “Broadway Basie’s Way,” and “Hollywood Basie’s Way,” two separate albums on Command Records. Byron has them. He thinks they’re great Basie records, ‘cause Roy Eldridge was on one of them. And they have taken them both, and they’ve put them, I think Decca bought them up, and they’ve put them into a double album. I’m not talking CD now, I’m talking about LP. And a couple of years ago I spotted it in a store called…

me playing.” He said “I thought it was Sonny Payne.” I says “that’s a nice compliment, but no that’s me, I made “‘Strangers in the Night.’” So they have no idea whether it’s me, and for people that don’t know Lockjaw Davis, who was a great tenor player at the time with the band, they won’t know it’s Roy Eldridge unless they know their jazz history. So I’m giving a very long answer I hope you don’t mind but you’re absolutely right, when they don’t list personnel, and they don’t even list the period of time when it…
